# How far can a phone camera go toward a spectrum?

A phone camera records three numbers per pixel, so it cannot measure a 27-band spectrum directly. This study asks how well a calibrated camera could estimate one, by simulating cameras on real measured reflectance. The main results use a DSLR's measured color curves, and measured curves from six iPhones, up to the 12 Pro Max, gave similar answers.

With calibration on hundreds of similar objects measured by spectrometer, 83% of 532 samples of natural objects met both draft targets. With only a 24-patch color chart, 60% did. When the light changed and nothing corrected for it, 0–34% did, and a white reference card brought that back to 52–59%. Using a screen as an extra light added almost nothing at the median. With the iPhone curves, the first two figures were 84–86% and 61–64%.

**No phone photo and no wild fungus was tested. Never use this to decide whether a mushroom is safe to eat.**

| Condition | Share meeting both draft targets |  |
|---|---|---|
| Calibrated on hundreds of similar objects measured by spectrometer | 83% | 95% interval 80–86% |
| Calibrated on a 24-patch color chart | 60% | 95% interval 56–64% |
| Light changed, no correction | 0–34% | Range across 6 lights |
| Light changed, white card | 52–59% | Range across 6 lights |

Share of held-out samples meeting both draft targets: spectral angle at most 10° and mean absolute error (MAE) at most 0.05. Angle measures the spectrum's shape. MAE measures reflectance error, so 0.05 is 5 percentage points. The targets are placeholders, not validated limits.

## 1. In this simulation, changed light hurt most, and a white card recovered most of the loss

Calibrating on a chart under flash and then shooting under other light dropped the share meeting both targets from 60% to 0–34%. A gain correction from one white patch in the same scene brought it back to 52–59%. Photographing the whole chart under that light reached 58–63%.

Against the study's 20% bar, the white card cleared it under 4 of 6 lights. It missed under daylight and fluorescent light, where there was less to recover. The full chart cleared it under all 6.

*Share of samples meeting both targets, by light*

|  | No correction | White card | Chart under that light |
|---|---|---|---|
| D65 daylight | 29% | 54% | 60% |
| A incandescent | 0% | 52% | 63% |
| LED-B1 warm white | 1% | 52% | 60% |
| LED-B5 cool white | 27% | 57% | 58% |
| FL2 fluorescent | 34% | 58% | 59% |
| Green shade | 13% | 59% | 61% |

*Caveat: This assumes one light falling evenly on the card and the object. Dappled light under a canopy is not modeled, and the green shade is an illustrative stand-in.*

## 2. Measured spectra are harder than the first demo suggested

The app's first version reported a median spectral angle of 2.25° because it tested spectra generated by the same model its solver assumes. On measured spectra, with a real camera's measured sensitivity, the same kind of fit gives 5.28° on natural objects and 8.81° on an exploratory mixed set of 190 samples.

The typical error is small, but the tail is long: the worst natural-object sample reached 28°.

*Median spectral angle, one photo under flash*

|  | Value |
|---|---|
| First demo: generated spectra | 2.25° |
| Natural objects, measured | 5.28° |
| Mixed set, measured | 8.81° |

## 3. Measured iPhone curves gave results close to the Nikon's

With the Nikon D5100's measured sensitivities and a linear fit, 83% of samples met both targets, and 60% with chart-only calibration. Measured curves from six iPhones gave 84–86% and 61–64%. The 12 Pro Max, the newest available, gave 85% (95% interval 82–88) and 62%.

Under the plan's rule, a Nikon conclusion holds if it has the same outcome on at least 5 of the 6 phones. Those on the hard limit, chart transfer and screen light hold. The two per-light conclusions don't hold exactly: the white card cleared the bar under 4 or 5 of 6 lights, and the full chart under 5 or 6, so the pattern is close but not identical.

Other curves can behave differently. The Sigma SD Merrill, with a layered Foveon sensor, gave 56%. A nonlinear fit on the Nikon gave 90%, and a constant spectrum, the baseline to beat, 7%.

*Share of samples meeting both targets, by camera curves*

|  | Calibrated on similar objects | Color chart only |

| Nikon D5100 | 83% | 60% |
| iPhone 6s | 84% | 61% |
| iPhone SE | 86% | 64% |
| iPhone 8 | 84% | 61% |
| iPhone X | 84% | 62% |
| iPhone 11 | 85% | 62% |
| iPhone 12 Pro Max | 85% | 62% |

## 4. A nonlinear model does better, but whether three numbers are a hard limit is unresolved

The study's test for a hard limit was whether a nonlinear model lowers median MAE by more than 10%. On natural objects it did so by 16%, but the 95% interval (5–21%) spans that line, so this stays unresolved. On the exploratory mixed set the gain was 18% (11–28%). On mushrooms it was 1%.

A nonlinear fit on one photo also beat a linear fit on four photos at the median (0.0103 against 0.0125). The chart's lower bars show the best linear summaries for scale. They don't bound what a nonlinear model could do. The repeat error is how much the reference measurements themselves differ, taken in similar regions of each object.

*Median MAE on natural objects, lower is better*

|  | Value |
|---|---|
| Camera, linear fit | 0.0122 |
| Camera, nonlinear fit | 0.0103 |
| Best 3 numbers, known exactly | 0.0081 |
| Repeat-measurement error | 0.0058 |
| Best 5 numbers, known exactly | 0.0051 |

## 5. Using a screen as extra light added almost nothing at the median

Each screen color was exposed so its strongest channel matched flash on a white target, with three times the noise because a screen is dimmer. Adding three screen colors to the flash changed median MAE by 0% (−3 to 2). The tail did improve: 90th percentile MAE fell from 0.037 to 0.028, and the share meeting both targets rose from 83% to 86%. With chart-only calibration the drop was 10% (8 to 11), and the share rose from 60% to 71%. No arm cleared the 20% bar on natural objects.

Screen colors alone did worse than flash (−22% (−25 to −19)). Steady daylight as a second light gave 10% (9 to 11). Three flash brightness levels gave 9% (8 to 10); they add no independent measurements, so that gain comes from averaging noise.

On mushrooms, brightness levels (36%) and steady daylight (24%) cleared the bar with calibration on similar samples. With a chart alone, the daylight and screen arms made mushrooms worse (-39%, -29% and -16%).

What moved the natural-object result: lower noise gave 15%, screen photos as clean as flash gave 17%, five times the screen noise gave -5%, narrow screen colors gave 5%, wide ones -1%, and the measured curves of an older Apple display 1%. Only the Sigma camera's curves cleared the bar (44%).

*Share of samples meeting both targets, by how the photos were taken*

|  | Calibrated on similar objects | Color chart only |
|---|---|---|
| Flash only | 83% | 60% |
| Three flash brightness levels | 85% | 61% |
| Flash plus steady daylight | 87% | 60% |
| Screen red, green, blue | 77% | 58% |
| Flash plus screen red, green, blue | 86% | 71% |

*Capture arms, calibrated on similar objects*

| Capture | Numbers recorded | Independent directions | Median MAE | 90th percentile MAE | Worst MAE | Median per-sample drop in MAE (95% interval) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flash only | 3 | 3 | 0.0122 | 0.037 | 0.084 | Baseline |
| Three flash brightness levels | 9 | 3 | 0.0108 | 0.036 | 0.085 | 9% (8 to 10) |

| Screen red, green, blue | 9 | 6 | 0.0151 | 0.038 | 0.082 | −22% (−25 to −19) |
| Flash plus screen red, green, blue | 12 | 9 | 0.0125 | 0.028 | 0.063 | 0% (−3 to 2) |

*Caveat: Screen colors other than that older display are illustrative, because no measured iPhone screen curve was available. Only a real phone test can settle this.*

## 6. A color chart transfers unevenly

Calibrating on the chart alone raised median MAE by 43% overall, past the study's 20% limit. It held up on flowers and fruits. On leaves the error was 3.8 times that of a calibration on leaves, and only 13% of leaf samples met both targets, against 99%. On bark the error was 2.7 times, and on mushrooms 1.8 times.

*Median MAE by kind of object, lower is better*

|---|---|---|
| Leaves (114) | 0.005 | 0.019 |
| Barks (20) | 0.005 | 0.013 |
| Stones (63) | 0.008 | 0.015 |
| Birds (105) | 0.009 | 0.015 |
| Butterflies (53) | 0.010 | 0.013 |
| Flowers (113) | 0.027 | 0.032 |
| Fruits (31) | 0.022 | 0.023 |
| Plant fruits (15) | 0.018 | 0.016 |
| Beetles (9) | 0.019 | 0.017 |

*Caveat: Beetles and vegetables have only 9 samples each, so their same-kind results are unstable.*

## 7. The mushroom data cannot answer the mushroom question

The only public mushroom reflectance data found covers 250 samples. The source does not name the species, and dry matter runs from 6% to 87%. Their spectra barely change shape. One number gets a median MAE of 0.0063, and a constant spectrum already meets the angle target on every sample (median 1.47°).

So the 100% meeting both targets here says little. Wild fungi with varied pigments remain untested.

## 8. Look-alikes are real but rare, and mostly dark

Of 140,847 pairs of samples from different species or specimens, 1,510 looked alike under flash at this noise level, and 202 of those differed by more than a draft target. Most of that is shape in dark patches: 199 exceeded the angle target alone, only 3 exceeded the MAE target, and 199 include a patch with mean reflectance below 0.15. Screen light would separate 3 of the 202.

An example: a purple plum and a black tourmaline stone. Their simulated flash responses are nearly the same, yet their spectra differ in shape by 25°. The difference in reflectance is small, 0.026 on average.

## 9. The app's first “95%” intervals were not 95%

An interval labeled 95% from the original session bootstrap contained the truth about 50% of the time with 2 sessions, and 75% with 3. Ignoring sessions, the original default, stayed near 81% however many sessions were added.

The app now uses exact order-statistic intervals that state their true level: 75% for 3 sessions, and at least 95% from 6 sessions. They are wider, and that is the price of few sessions.

*How often an interval contained the truth*

| Number of sessions | Exact interval (states its level) | Session bootstrap (labeled 95%) | Ignoring sessions (labeled 95%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 50% | 50% | 78% |

| 4 | 87% | 82% | 80% |
| 5 | 95% | 84% | 83% |
| 6 | 97% | 86% | 82% |
| 8 | 99% | 90% | 82% |
| 12 | 96% | 92% | 83% |
| 20 | 97% | 94% | 84% |

*Caveat: Simulated with 5 specimens per session and sessions making up 36% of the variance. Other scenarios are in results/coverage.json.*

## What this does not show

- No phone photo was used. RGB values are simulated from the measured curves of two DSLRs and six iPhones, none newer than the 12 Pro Max.
- The noise model is simple. It leaves out clipping, tone mapping, uneven light, gloss and viewing angle, so real results should be expected to be worse.
- Calibrating on similar objects takes hundreds of spectrometer readings, which most people do not have.
- The spectra come from specific collections: natural objects from one region of Argentina, and mushrooms of an unnamed species. Other materials may behave differently.
- The draft targets are placeholders. Meeting them is not evidence of fitness for any purpose.
- No human expert has reviewed this work.
- Nothing here identifies a species, and nothing here supports a decision about eating anything.
- The first idea behind this project included 3D capture. No 3D work is reported here; the code contains only a tested point-projection function.

## What would settle more of this

- Run the phone test. It needs no purchase and measures how stable a real phone is. It may also show whether screen light adds real measurements, though the simulation says that needs many objects.
- Measure a current iPhone's color curves and its flash spectrum, and repeat this study with them.
- Pair phone photos with spectrometer readings of the same marked spots, starting with stable matte targets. Only that can test spectral accuracy.

## How this was done

The analysis plan was written before the natural-object and mushroom results were computed. It has no independent timestamp. A separate AI code review of the first full run found a flaw in how screen light was modeled, which erased most of the first reported gain. That and every other change are listed at the end of study/PLAN.md. No human expert has reviewed this work yet.

The plan is in [study/PLAN.md](../study/PLAN.md), the raw numbers are in [results/](../results/), and the data sources are in [DATA.md](DATA.md).
